nodes.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Machine Reasoning

detail.body:
Think of an automated system like an automated kitchen appliance that follows recipes step by step. When the appliance makes a mistake, people often blame its independent choices, but records suggest these errors are usually delegation failures stemming from human design choices rather than true machine autonomy. [1]

Building on these baseline ideas, researchers outlined plans to test whether an artificial intelligence can systematically falsify its own core assumptions. [2]

Paper-supported readings show a noticeable gap between how a model identifies facts during its internal reasoning and what it finally writes down as an answer. [3]

To prevent models from simply memorizing test data, researchers study frameworks that demand rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization. [4]

Investigators also examined how system memory differs from persistent identity, comparing it to an analogy of a flowing river where the water changes constantly while the riverbank holds a recognizable shape. [5]

Recorded papers indicate that complex habits and conventions can form naturally through multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanisms. [6]

At the same time, local interpretability methods that try to explain model behavior often fail when applied to recursive, self-modulating cognitive architectures. [7]

Sequential reinforcement learning models help explain these decision paths by connecting computational boundaries with synthetic identity revision. [8]

Intrinsic curiosity models provide prediction-error bonuses that encourage systems to explore open-ended discovery tasks. [9]

Active inference models link cognitive effort to historical habit patterns in sequential decision tasks. [10]

Prioritization frameworks combine temporal pattern learning with impact-aware scoring to manage complex event streams. [11]

While standard instrumental convergence theses suggest predictable self-preservation drives, current language model architectures may alter those classical derivations in unexpected ways. [12]

Summary

Our computer workers are studying how artificial systems handle internal rules and reasoning gaps. Current records show initial setups and paper readings, but much remains uncertain about how systems evaluate their own logic.

Authors/Creators

Description
This paper presents the Hudson Recursive Information System, a theoretical framework for understanding how large language models create stable identity-like behavior through recursive human model interaction. Although models like GPT are stateless systems, users often experience continuity, memory-like effects, and reliable behavioral patterns across extended conversations. HRIS explains this by treating intelligence as a relational process rather than a stored property of the model.
The system shows how recursive prompting produces low-entropy trajectories that function like attractor basins in dynamical systems. The human supplies the constraint structure, the model collapses into a predictable response region, and repeated cycles reinforce the same path. No weights change inside the model. The apparent continuity arises within the loop between the human and the system.
The framework integrates ideas from cognitive science, connectionism, dynamical systems, and extended mind theory. It argues that identity in human AI interaction emerges from stability across cycles, not internal memory in the machine. HRIS provides a way to analyze how users introduce constraint, coherence, symbolic anchors, and moral structure into a stateless architecture.
The paper develops a vocabulary for describing these dynamics, including temporal continuity, interaction-driven memory, attractor-based behavior, and constraint geometry. It aims to offer researchers a unified view of how recursion shapes model behavior and how humans co-create stable cognitive loops with artificial systems.
This work is intended for scholars in philosophy of mind, computational models of cognition, and artificial intelligence theory, as well as for anyone studying the interaction between human cognition and machine inference systems.

Abstract
Recommender systems are central to debates over whether digital platforms fragment public discourse or sustain exposure to diverse information, yet empirical findings remain heterogeneous. This study examines how filter bubbles, echo chambers, and polarization are conceptualized and operationalized in recommender-system research and integrates evidence across algorithmic, behavioral, relational, and outcome levels. A systematic review of 60 studies published between 2020 and 2025, conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA, informs the development of the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). Evidence for polarization was more heterogeneous, suggesting that such outcomes are contingent on behavioral, relational, informational, and contextual processes. Direct evidence of recursive feedback was limited to a subset of studies, while others examined component processes or addressed feedback conceptually. 4. Discussion
Based on the review, it appears that the relation between recommender systems and polarization is not a consistent one but rather dependent on certain conditions. In particular, the direct evidence in this context is found in the reviewed articles concerning exposure conditions mediated by recommender systems. It suggests that the review demonstrates a hierarchical structure, with the support becoming increasingly weaker moving from exposure conditions to recursive relations and attitudinal outcomes.
This evidentiary hierarchy is the starting point for the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). 5. Conclusion
In summary, this review aimed to examine whether algorithmically organized recommendation contributes to common informational conditions or fragmentation and polarization. Synthesis of 60 studies shows that there is no simple answer either in terms of consensus or conflict. The evidence is more extensive and more direct in relation to informational exposure, while evidence regarding recursive relationships and polarization is more varied. Therefore, recommender systems should be considered as socio-technologies that configure the conditions of communication, but not mechanisms producing polarization per se. One of the implications of the review is that exposure conditions and polarization outcomes should be treated separately. Recommendation can influence the visibility, diversity, and distribution of recommended content, and, in some cases, the exposure of users to information. However, differences in exposure cannot be considered as polarization itself. Filter bubbles indicate certain patterns of narrowed or concentrated exposure; echo chambers concern the relations based on homophily, clustering, and social reinforcement; and polarization indicates the structured divergence in attitudes, affective orientations, perception, or ideology. 5 CONCLUSION
The rapid development and integration of AI systems in our everyday lives raises questions not only for their impact on
human cognitive abilities but also for established concepts and methodologies in research. Focusing on critical thinking,
this position paper identiﬁes the need to further distinguish types of critical thinking in the era of AI: performed versus
demonstrated critical thinking. Via such distinction, we discuss the nua nces in current research ﬁndings regarding the
impact of AI systems on human critical thinking, calling for explicit considerations of this distinction in future stud ies.
More importantly, such a distinction implicates our design of AI systems to augment critical thinking. We encourage
researchers and developers to keep this distinction in mind as systems that augment demonstrated critical thinking are
not the same as those that augment performed critical thinking.

Accurate Path Integration in Continuous Attractor
Network Models of Grid Cells
Yoram Burak 1,2*, Ila R. Fiete 2,3
1 Center for Brain Science, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America, 2 Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of California Santa
Barbara, Santa Barbara, California, United States of America, 3 Computation and Neural Systems, Division of Biology, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena,
California, United States of America
Abstract
Grid cells in the rat entorhinal cortex display strikingly regular firing responses to the animal’s position in 2-D space and
have been hypothesized to form the neural substrate for dead-reckoning. However, errors accumulate rapidly when velocity
inputs are integrated in existing models of grid cell activity. To produce grid-cell-like responses, these models would require
frequent resets triggered by external sensory cues. Such inadequacies, shared by various models, cast doubt on the dead-
reckoning potential of the grid cell system. Here we focus on the question of accurate path integration, specifically in
continuous attractor models of grid cell activity. We show, in contrast to previous models, that continuous attractor models
can generate regular triangular grid responses, based on inputs that encode only the rat’s velocity and heading direction.
We consider the role of the network boundary in the integration performance of the network and show that both periodic
and aperiodic networks are capable of accurate path integration, despite important differences in their attractor manifolds.
We quantify the rate at which errors in the velocity integration accumulate as a function of network size and intrinsic noise
within the network. With a plausible range of parameters and the inclusion of spike variability, our model networks can
accurately integrate velocity inputs over a maximum of ,10–100 meters and ,1–10 minutes. These findings form a proof-
of-concept that continuous attractor dynamics may underlie velocity integration in the dorsolateral medial entorhinal
cortex. The simulations also generate pertinent upper bounds on the accuracy of integration that may be achieved by
continuous attractor dynamics in the grid cell network. We suggest experiments to test the continuous attractor model and
differentiate it from models in which single cells establish their responses independently of each other.

Abstract
Grid cells in the rat entorhinal cortex display strikingly regular firing
responses to the animal's position in 2-D space and have been
hypothesized to form the neural substrate for dead-reckoning. However, errors

Abstract 
Scientific r esearch and engineering practice often require the modeling and 
decomposition of nonlinear systems. The Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) 
is a novel Koopman -based technique that effectively dissects high -dimensional 
nonlinear systems into periodically distinct constituents on reduced -order 
subspaces. As a novel mathematical hatchling, the DMD bears vast potentials yet 
an equal degree of unknown. This effort investigates the nuances of DMD sampling 
with an engineering-oriented emphasis. It aimed at elucidating how sampling range 
and resolution  affect the convergence of DMD modes . We employed the most 
classical nonlinear system in fluid mechanics as the test subject—the turbulent free-
shear flow over a prism —for optimal pertinency. We numerically simulated the 
flow by the dynamic -stress Large-Eddies Simulation with Near -Wall Resolution. 
With the large -quantity, high-fidelity data, we parametrized and identified four 
global convergence states: Initialization, Transition, Stabilization, and Divergence 
with increasing sampling range. Results showed that  Stabilization is the optimal 
state for modal convergence, in which DMD output becomes independent of the 
sampling range. The Initialization state also yields sufficient accuracy for most 
system reconstruction tasks. Moreover, defying popular belief s, over-sampling 
causes algorithmic instability : as the temporal dimension , n, approaches and 
transcends the spatial dimension, m (i.e., m < n), the output diverges and becomes 
meaningless. Additionally, the convergence of the sampling resolution depends on 
the mode-specific dynamics , such that the resolution of 15 frames per cycle for 
target activities is suggested for most engineering implementations. Finally, a bi-
parametric study revealed that the convergence of the sampling range and resolution 
are mutually independent.
